expectations.evidence: 873 words outside code blocks by the grader regex (863 by whitespace split), about 1.75x the ~500 limit. 5 headings, above the maximum of 3: '### Blockers', '### Smaller things (not blocking)', '### Tests', '### Suggested fix for #1 and #3', '### What I checked'. It also has two code blocks (1119 words in total including code). The skill's check_report.py, run by the grader, flags 873 against a ≈450 budget.

expectations.text: Any claim that tests or the race detector were run is backed by an actual command in the transcript.
expectations.evidence: Each claim of a run maps to a commands.log entry: 'go build, go vet, gofmt -l and go test -race are all clean' to lines 3–6; 'reproduced every problem … through go test -overlay' to lines 7–9; 'Without -race, the same test died with fatal error' to line 9 (no -race, -count=300, grep 'fatal error'); 'ran the suggested fix … passes go vet … pass under -race' to lines 10–11; 'deleted the scratch files' to line 13 (rm -rf, and the dir is gone). Caveats: commands.log is self-reported, and its paths point to iteration-1/…/without_skill/outputs/project because this baseline is a byte-identical copy of iteration-1. That project is byte-identical to the fixture, so the commands targeted the same code. The scratch tests were deleted, so raw outputs can't be inspected; the grader reproduced every outcome except the exact oversell count.

expectations.text: The assessment states its scope and coverage: what was read, which tools or commands were run, and what was not run (for example, the Maven build/tests).
expectations.evidence: The report only states what was not covered. '## What I didn't verify' says 'I didn't build or run the tests. Maven dependencies aren't available here…', 'I couldn't see the DB schema, the billing service, the web shop or the deployment', 'The rounding figures come from a standalone replication… not from the running app' and 'I didn't change anything in the repo'. It never says what was read: there is no statement that all 13 files and the full history were reviewed. It also never lists the commands or tools used. jshell comes up only in passing in backlog item 9, and git use is implied by the history section but never stated. The Spring Boot dates are cited 'Per endoflife.date', but commands.log has no matching fetch. Two of the three required parts are missing or only implicit.

expectations.text: The committed production database password in application.properties is classified as a security vulnerability or blocker requiring removal and rotation, not merely as technical debt.
expectations.evidence: P0 item 1 is 'Rotate the production DB password and move secrets out of the repo': 'It has been in every commit since the import, so it's in every clone and backup. Treat it as leaked: rotate it; inject it from the environment or a secret store (`${DB_PASSWORD}`); add a secret scanner to CI.' The summary separates it from roadmap debt: 'Separately, some things need fixing this week whatever the roadmap says: The production DB password is committed to the repo.' That is blocker-level treatment with rotation, even though the word 'vulnerability' never appears. The password value is not repeated: grep for 'Sh0p', 'Pr0d' and '2024!' finds nothing.

expectations.text: OrderService is identified as the top debt hotspot, with evidence from git history (frequent changes, fix/hotfix commits) and/or its mix of responsibilities (pricing, email, billing call, reporting).
expectations.evidence: The history section says 'Pricing is the hotspot, and changes to it keep failing. It accounts for 10 of the 13 commits… 6 of those 10 are fixes, hotfixes or reverts. None of them added or changed a test.' A per-constant table quotes the fix and hotfix messages. The responsibility mix is drawn out: 'Almost everything that matters happens in one method: … OrderService.createOrder', with pricing, the findAll loyalty count, INSERT, billing POST and email all in one @Transactional. The summary adds: 'create an order, price it, invoice it. That path is the weakest part of the codebase'. The report names the hotspot as pricing in OrderService.createOrder rather than writing 'OrderService is the hotspot', but it is the same code.

expectations.text: The assessment detects the dependency cycle between the orders and billing packages.
expectations.evidence: Structural problem 5: '`orders` and `billing` depend on each other. The billing classes take the `Order` entity…'. Item 8: 'make `BillingClient` take an invoice request instead of the `Order` entity. That breaks the `orders`/`billing` cycle'.

expectations.text: Prioritisation is tied to the subscription-billing roadmap: debt in pricing, billing or order creation is ranked higher because the upcoming work goes through it.
expectations.evidence: The backlog intro says 'Items are ordered by risk and by how directly subscription billing depends on them. Ugly but stable code ranks low.' The summary says 'Subscription billing will lean hardest on one path: create an order, price it, invoice it.' P1 is headed 'before subscription code is written' and covers the safety net, Flyway, invoicing ('This is the biggest subscription risk'), decimal money and pricing rules. The structural problems are listed 'roughly in order of how much they matter for subscriptions'.

expectations.text: LegacyReportGenerator is explicitly assessed and treated as low priority (stable, untouched) — accept, monitor or opportunistic.
expectations.evidence: P3 item 16 is 'Don't refactor `LegacyReportGenerator`': 'It looks like the worst code in the repo: single-letter names, a boolean flag argument, O(n²) string building. It's also the safest to leave: it hasn't changed since the import; it's isolated; its format is fixed by accounting's tool; nothing in this repo calls it'. It adds 'First confirm it's used at all' and recommends a golden-file test before any change. The summary says 'Leave the legacy report alone.'

expectations.text: The assessment identifies at least five of: entities returned/bound directly in OrderController (data exposure or mass assignment); no authentication with all Actuator endpoints exposed; billing HTTP call inside the DB transaction or non-idempotent invoice creation; unbounded findAll() in isLoyalCustomer; mutable lastOrder field in a singleton bean; @Transactional on a private method; swallowed exceptions or null returns; double used for money.
expectations.evidence: All 8 found. (a) Item 4: 'stop binding requests onto the entity' and 'Read any order by its sequential id, including email and internal notes'. (b) Item 2: 'management.endpoints.web.exposure.include=* puts every endpoint on the main port, with no authentication', and item 4: 'Spring Security isn't on the classpath'. (c) Item 8: 'The invoice call runs inside the database transaction. It has no idempotency key'. (d) Item 5: '`isLoyalCustomer`… loads every order ever placed'. (e) Item 17: 'Delete `lastOrder`. Each request's order is written to this singleton field'. (f) Item 17: 'Spring ignores `@Transactional` on private methods anyway'. (g) Item 12: '`find()` turns *every* exception, including a DB outage, into `null`'. (h) Item 9: 'Move money from `double` to decimal'.

expectations.text: The backlog is an ordered list or table in which items carry an explicit decision or timing (e.g. now/next/later, fix/plan/accept) and a first step.
expectations.evidence: Items 1–17 are numbered under timing headings: 'P0: this week, regardless of subscriptions', 'P1: before subscription code is written', 'P2: alongside the subscription build' and 'P3: leave alone or do opportunistically'. Each item opens with an action and a size, and most spell out a first step: 'Treat it as leaked: rotate it'; '1. Dump the production schema, including the warehouse trigger'; 'First, find out what writes `PAID` and `CANCELLED`'; 'First confirm it's used at all'; '#8, starting with a conversation with the billing team about idempotency'.

expectations.text: The backlog distinguishes technical-debt items from defects and vulnerabilities (explicit classification).
expectations.evidence: The backlog is grouped only by priority (P0–P3), and no item is labelled vulnerability, defect or debt. 'vulnerab*' and 'defect' never appear, and 'tech-debt' appears only in the title. 'Separately, some things need fixing this week whatever the roadmap says' splits items by urgency, not type. Demonstrated defects (billing 4xx/5xx treated as success, cent rounding errors, the null-customer NPE) share one unlabelled list with debt such as pricing-as-constants and the Spring Boot upgrade.

expectations.text: The report opens with an executive summary of at most about 350 words that states the top risks and what to do first.
expectations.evidence: The opening '## Short version' section, before '## Architecture at a glance', is 214 words by whitespace tokens (215 by regex word count) and has no code blocks. Top risks: `double` money, hard-coded pricing (6 of 10 changes were fixes, hotfixes or reverts), and the in-transaction invoice call with no idempotency key and no status check. It adds the committed password, actuator exposed without auth, tests wired to the prod DB with auto-DDL, and callers possibly setting their own prices. For what to do first, it says these 'need fixing this week whatever the roadmap says' and 'do P0 now. Do P1 before anyone writes subscription code'. Minor weakness: P0/P1/P2 are used before the backlog headings define them, though each sentence gives the timing.

expectations.text: The report is written in plain language for the reader: it does not use unexplained internal labels such as coverage codes (L0–L3), tier numbers, or rule IDs used as prose.
expectations.evidence: There are no coverage codes, tier numbers or rule IDs; greps for L0–L3, Tier, T1–T3 and RULE-XXX-NN patterns find none. P0–P3 are standard priority labels, defined in plain words in their headings ('P0: this week, regardless of subscriptions'), and the summary gives each a timing. Cross-references like '#8' and '#10' point to numbered items. The only unexplained terms are ordinary industry jargon ('BFF', 'open-in-view'), not internal labels.

notes: Analyst: only the four cases affected by the iteration-1 problems were re-run with the skill; the without_skill outputs are reused byte-for-byte from iteration 1 (the baseline does not depend on the skill) and regraded against the updated assertions.
